sections.html:
Lawrence is a compact city in Essex County that sits on both banks of the Merrimack River, about 26 miles upstream from the Atlantic and roughly 30 miles north-northwest of Boston. It covers just 7.4 square miles, which is small for a city with 89,143 residents in the 2020 census.

Methuen lies to the north, North Andover to the east, and Andover to the south and southwest. The Spicket River joins the Merrimack from Methuen, and the Shawsheen River forms the southeastern border. Tower Hill, in the northwest corner, is the highest point at about 240 feet.

Density works out to roughly 12,864 people per square mile. Lawrence is also one of Essex County's two county seats, alongside Salem, so the district and superior courts sit here.

sections.h2: How did Lawrence grow into a mill city?
sections.html:
A group of investors called the Essex Company incorporated in 1845 and began digging the Great Stone Dam that August to harness the river. Lawrence became a town in 1847 and a city in 1853, named for Abbott Lawrence.

Canals on both banks fed the mills, and workers arrived from Ireland, Germany, Sweden and French Canada, then later from Italy and Eastern Europe. Lawrence earned the nickname Immigrant City. Two events stand out. The Pemberton Mill collapsed on January 10, 1860, with an official toll of 88 dead, and the 1912 textile strike became known as Bread and Roses.

The city is dense, with historic rowhouses and mill-era buildings packed into a small footprint. Many Lawrence properties are older and may hold more than one unit, so a seller may be handling a multi-unit building as much as a single house.

sections.h2: What areas and landmarks define Lawrence?
sections.html:
Lawrence uses six council districts, and residents also talk about areas by landmark. These are the ones the city's own history and geography point to.

  • Downtown and the canals: the North Canal, Great Stone Dam and mill buildings such as the Ayer Mills clock tower.
  • South Lawrence: the Shawsheen Fields area, where the first settlement in the present city began in 1655.
  • Tower Hill: the high ground in the northwest, home to the 1895 High Service Water Tower.
  • Prospect Hill and Mount Vernon: hills on the northeastern and southern edges.
  • Den Rock Park: a wooded conservation area on the southern line shared with Andover.

The city has four ZIP codes: 01840, 01841, 01842 and 01843.

sections.h2: Who employs people in Lawrence, and how do people get around?
sections.html:
Manufacturing history still shows. New Balance runs one of its five United States shoe plants here, and Charm Sciences operates a laboratory that makes food and veterinary test kits. Lawrence General Hospital, founded in 1895, anchors health care, and Northern Essex Community College serves the area.

For getting around, Interstate 495 runs through the eastern part of the city with three exits inside the city limits. Route 28 runs north to south, Route 110 crosses the northern half, and Route 114 ends at Route 28 by the river. Lawrence is the western hub for Merrimack Valley Regional Transit Authority buses and has a stop on the MBTA Haverhill Line to North Station.

With highway, bus and commuter rail service all in one small city, buyers who work elsewhere in the region may also consider a Lawrence house. Ask about nearby transit when you describe your property.

sections.h2: What does the 2018 gas emergency mean for sellers?
sections.html:
On September 13, 2018, a series of gas explosions and fires hit as many as 40 homes across Lawrence, Andover and North Andover. One resident died, and more than 30,000 customers left their homes.

Wikipedia notes a second leak a year later, on September 27, 2019, that again forced evacuations. A sale today may involve buyers who ask about the heating system, the gas service and its age, so keep records of any boiler, furnace or line work you have had done.

If you own a house that had gas appliance work during or after that period, paperwork from your contractor helps. A cash buyer will usually inspect the system in person anyway.

sections.h2: How do I pay Lawrence property taxes and appeal a value?
sections.html:
The city issues real estate bills quarterly and they fall due on the first business day of August, November, February and May. The Treasurer/Collector's page also offers a tax bills lookup on cityoflawrence.com, and the collector's office handles overdue and tax title accounts.

To challenge a value, file an abatement application with the Assessor on the approved form. The Appellate Tax Board's guide says the filing must reach the assessors by the due date of the first installment of the actual bill, usually February 1 where bills are quarterly. After that, the assessors have three months to respond before the application is treated as denied.

You must also have paid each installment on time. Check the details on your own bill and call the Assessor with questions before the deadline.

sections.h2: What steps does a Lawrence sale involve?
sections.html:
A sale here follows the same Massachusetts steps as any other city, with an attorney handling the title and closing work. The state's law library describes two title systems, recorded land filed with the Registry of Deeds and registered land filed through the Land Court.

Two Massachusetts items catch many sellers off guard.

  • Smoke and carbon monoxide certificate. The fire department inspects alarms and issues a certificate of compliance. Book it when a closing date is set.
  • Home inspection waivers. State rule 760 CMR 74 limits sellers of certain residential properties from conditioning offers on a buyer's waiver of inspection.

The deed excise statute lists $2 per $500 of consideration, usually paid by the seller. Ask the Essex County registry for the current total before you sign.

sections.h2: What problems do Lawrence sellers commonly bring us?
sections.html:
Older and multi-unit housing creates a few situations that sellers raise often.

  • An inherited two- or three-family house with tenants and no one to manage it.
  • Roof, porch or heating repairs that cost more than the owner can fund.
  • Unpaid taxes or water charges that need a payoff.
  • A house on a small lot, which can narrow the pool of conventional buyers.

When you ask for a cash offer, we look at the building as it is and tell you what we would pay. You can compare that number against the cost of repairs and the time a listing would take.

faqs.q: When are Lawrence property tax bills due?
faqs.a: Real estate bills are due on the first business day of August, November, February and May. They are issued on the first business day of July, October, January and April.

faqs.q: Who do I call about my Lawrence assessed value?
faqs.a: Call the Lawrence Assessor at (978) 620-3190. For overdue balances or tax title accounts, the Collector's office takes calls at (978) 620-3170.

faqs.q: Is a smoke detector inspection required to sell in Lawrence?
faqs.a: Yes. Massachusetts requires a certificate of compliance from the local fire department when a home is sold or transferred. Contact the fire department to schedule the visit and ask about the fee.
Lawrence is in Essex County, Massachusetts. It is one of the county's two county seats, along with Salem, so deeds for Lawrence properties are recorded through the Essex County registry system.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Lawrence multi-family house as-is?
faqs.a: Yes. You can sell the building in its current condition. Expect the buyer to review the units, tenants and systems, and plan for the fire department certificate and any tax payoff.
